876.title: Seek, do, teach (Ezra 7:10)
876.hook: Ezra the scribe set his heart to seek the law, do it, and teach it
876.carry: study begins as a direction you set inside
876.howItsDone: A sofer is a trained Jewish scribe who writes Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot by hand with a quill and ink on parchment, following detailed laws for every letter, and Ezra is remembered in Jewish tradition as Ezra the Scribe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sons of Asaph played, the old men wept, the crowd shouted, and no one could tell the sounds apart. Your line was weeping and joy together. Today, at last, Ezra himself.

The book that bears his name runs for chapters before Ezra himself walks in. When he does, the text slows down to introduce him: a long line of fathers, name after name, back to Aaron the chief priest. Then a job title. In the King James words: "he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the LORD God of Israel had given." He comes up from Babylon with the king's permission and a company of returning exiles, and the good hand of his God, the text says, was upon him. Then one sentence about what he set his heart on.
screen: `A LINE OF FATHERS, BACK TO AARON.` → `A READY SCRIBE.` → `UP FROM BABYLON.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments." Three verbs, in an order. Seek. The Hebrew verb is lidrosh, to search, to ask. Some readers hear in it the word midrash, the old Jewish way of searching a text for more than its surface. Ezra doesn't just read the law; he goes looking in it. Do. Before he teaches anyone, he does it himself; the verse puts the doing before a single word of teaching reaches anyone else. Teach. Only then does it go outward, to the people. And notice where it starts: he prepared his heart. Not his pen, not his scroll. Study begins as a direction you set inside. Today's word is what he was: a sofer, a scribe. The word is still in use. A sofer writes a Torah scroll by hand, letter by letter, with a quill on parchment, and tradition asks that a scroll for public reading be written that way, by someone who sits down and sets their heart to it.
screen: then, large: `SEEK IT, DO IT, TEACH IT.` · `DO IT BEFORE YOU TEACH IT.` · `HE PREPARED HIS HEART.` · then: `A SOFER STILL WRITES BY HAND.`

segments.voice: Take one line you trust, today's verse from Ezra or one from a book you keep near, and seek: turn it over and ask it one question. Then do: find one small, specific way to live it; then teach: think how you'd pass it on in a sentence. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition for a prepared heart.
Sofer. A scribe. Ezra was called a ready scribe in the law of Moses, and a sofer today still writes the Torah by hand. Today's word.
Your line: study begins as a direction you set inside. Seek, do, teach, in that order. Day eight hundred seventy-six, done.

877.title: A quick prayer, then speak (Nehemiah 2:1–5)
877.hook: the king's cupbearer prays silently, then makes his request
877.carry: the slow work was done before
877.howItsDone: Jewish tradition has set prayers for fixed times, and also short, personal prayers said in the moment; Nehemiah's silent prayer before answering the king is sometimes pointed to as an example of the second kind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezra the sofer, the scribe, set his heart to seek the teaching, do it, and teach it. Your line was study begins as a direction you set inside. Today, a different man in a different job: he pours the king's wine.

A cup of wine is on its way to a king. The man carrying it is Nehemiah, a Jew in exile, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia, in the palace at Shushan. He says he had never been sad in the king's presence before. But he has heard news from home: the wall of Jerusalem is broken down and its gates burned with fire. He wept, the book says, and fasted, and prayed. Now he hands over the cup, and the king sees his face. Why is your face sad, the king asks, when you aren't sick? This is nothing but sorrow of heart. Nehemiah writes that he was very much afraid.
screen: `THE KING'S CUPBEARER.` → `NEWS FROM HOME: THE WALL IS DOWN.` → `THE KING SEES HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Nehemiah answers honestly. Let the king live forever; why shouldn't my face be sad, when the city where my fathers are buried lies waste and its gates are burned? Then the king asks, in the King James words: "For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And the very next words: "And I said unto the king." No kneeling, no long speech. The king is waiting, and between the question and the answer Nehemiah prays. The book doesn't tell us the words. What it shows is the order: a quick prayer, then speak. And it isn't his only prayer. In chapter one he prayed at length, with fasting, confession and a long plea. The slow work was done before; the short prayer is what fits in the gap. Then Nehemiah speaks, and he's specific. If it please the king, send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may build it. He asks for letters for safe passage and for timber from the king's forest. And the king grants it, the text says, according to the good hand of God upon him. Today the king might be a manager, a doctor, a landlord, a parent. The gap between their question and your answer is short. Nehemiah shows what can fit inside it.

878.title: Build anyway (Nehemiah 4:11)
878.hook: the wall is rebuilt with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other
878.carry: one hand on the stone, one hand ready
878.howItsDone: Some Jewish readers turn to Nehemiah's builders, working with one hand and guarding with the other, as a picture of carrying on with a community's work under threat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nehemiah fit a whole prayer into one breath before the king. Your line was the slow work was done before. Today, he arrives in Jerusalem, and the work begins.

First come the jokes. Nehemiah has rallied the people, and they're raising the wall of Jerusalem on its old lines, family by family, each beside its own stretch. Across the way, the local strongmen Sanballat and Tobiah laugh. In the King James words, Sanballat sneers, "What do these feeble Jews?" Tobiah adds that if a fox went up on it, it would break their stone wall down. The jokes don't stop the work, so they turn into threats: a plan to come and fight against Jerusalem. Now the builders have a choice. Stop until it's safe, or find a way to keep going.
screen: `THE WALL GOES UP ON ITS OLD LINES.` → `FIRST THE MOCKERY.` → `THEN THE THREATS.`

segments.voice: Nehemiah does two things at once, side by side: "Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night." Prayer and a guard, together. Then he reorganizes the site. Half the young men work, half stand ready, with the people's leaders behind every section. And here is the picture this day is named for. The verse is numbered eleven in Hebrew Bibles and seventeen in the King James: "every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon." The builders wear swords at their sides while they lay brick. A man with a shofar, a ram's horn, stands next to Nehemiah, and the plan is simple: wherever you hear the horn, gather to us there; our God will fight for us. They work from first light until the stars come out. Nehemiah and his men don't even take off their clothes, except for washing. They don't wait for the threats to go away, and they don't pretend the threats aren't real. They hold both. Earlier, the text gives the reason the wall kept rising at all: the people had a mind to work. A hard week, a project people laugh at, a goal someone wants to stop: the wall in Nehemiah was built by people with only one hand free.
screen: `PRAYER AND A WATCH, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `ONE HAND WORKS, ONE HAND GUARDS.` · `GATHER WHERE THE SHOFAR SOUNDS.` · then: `THE PEOPLE HAD A MIND TO WORK.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up. Let one hand hold something you're building, a family, a habit, a piece of work, and the other whatever pushes against it, doubt, tiredness, a real worry, and ask what one brick you could still lay with both in hand. If you pray, bring both hands to God, the way Nehemiah's builders prayed and kept watch.
Build anyway. The wall of Jerusalem goes up with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, because the people had a mind to work. Today's word.

879.title: They gave the sense (Nehemiah 8:1–8)
879.hook: the people stand as Ezra reads, and Levites explain so everyone understands
879.howItsDone: In synagogue services the Torah is read aloud from the scroll, and teaching that explains the reading, through a sermon, a study session or a translation, is a familiar part of Jewish communal life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wall went up with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other. Your line was one hand on the stone, one hand ready. Today the wall is up, and the people gather to hear something read.

The request comes from the crowd. In the King James words, all the people gathered themselves together as one man into the street that was before the water gate. They ask Ezra the scribe, the same Ezra who set his heart to seek, do and teach: bring out the book of the law of Moses. So he brings it before the whole congregation, men and women, and everyone old enough to understand. He climbs a wooden platform built for the purpose, high enough to be seen, and opens the book, and all the people stand up. But a book read aloud isn't the same as a book understood.
screen: `THE PEOPLE ASK FOR THE BOOK.` → `EZRA ON A WOODEN PLATFORM.` → `THE BOOK OPENS. EVERYONE STANDS.`

segments.voice: Ezra blesses the LORD, and the people answer, Amen, Amen, lifting up their hands, then bowing with their faces to the ground. He reads from early morning until midday, and the ears of all the people were attentive. Then a detail that's easy to skip. Beside Ezra stands a list of named men, and with them the Levites, helping the people understand the teaching while they stand in their places. Then the verse this day is named for: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." Three steps. They read it distinctly, not rushed. They gave the sense: they explained what it meant. And they caused them to understand. The goal isn't that the words were said. It's that the people got it. The text doesn't say exactly how the Levites did it, whether they moved through the crowd, translated, or taught in small groups; readers have suggested each. What it does say is that reading alone wasn't counted as enough. People stood between the words and the listeners, building a bridge. A form, a diagnosis, a contract, a hard text: the words can all be there and still not land, until someone sits down and says, here's what this means.

In your mind, say it distinctly in plain words, then give the sense, why it matters, and trim one word you don't need. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition for clear speech and patient listening.
Sekhel. Ezra reads, the people stand, and the Levites explain until the reading is understood, with sekhel, good sense. Today's word.

880.title: Joy is your strength (Nehemiah 8:10)
880.hook: "the joy of the LORD is your strength"; eat, drink and send portions
880.howItsDone: Jewish festivals are kept with festive meals, and on Purim it is the custom to send gifts of food to friends and give to the poor, as the book of Esther describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezra read the teaching at the water gate, and the Levites gave the sekhel, the sense, so everyone understood. Your line was gave the sense. Today, what the people do once they understand.

The crowd is crying. All morning they've stood in the street and listened, and now that the words have been explained, they understand them. The text says it plainly: all the people wept when they heard the words of the law. Maybe they're hearing how far they've drifted. Maybe it's the weight of a whole people coming home. The book only says they wept. And then their leaders, Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites, do something unexpected. They don't tell them to cry harder. They tell them to stop.
screen: `THE WORDS ARE UNDERSTOOD.` → `ALL THE PEOPLE WEEP.` → `THE LEADERS SAY: STOP.`

segments.voice: This day is holy to the LORD your God, they say; don't mourn, and don't weep. Then comes an instruction that sounds like a party invitation. In the King James words: "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our LORD: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength." Eat the rich food. Drink the sweet drink. And send portions to the people who have nothing ready. The joy isn't private; it goes out the door on a plate. The Hebrew word for strength here is ma'oz, and some readers hear in it a stronghold, a place of refuge. On that reading, joy isn't only a feeling of being strong; it's a place to stand. Joy as a wall, in a book about building walls. The Levites quiet the people: hold your peace, for the day is holy; don't be grieved. And the people go off to eat and drink, send portions and make great rejoicing, the text says, because they had understood the words that were declared to them. The tears came from understanding, and so did the joy. Readers of the book of Esther may hear an echo here: Purim, too, is kept with feasting and with sending portions one to another.

881.title: From Adam (1 Chronicles 1)
881.hook: the Tanakh's last book begins with Adam and a list of generations
881.howItsDone: Jews read Chronicles as part of the Writings, the third section of the Tanakh; Jewish families also keep track of lineage in ways such as naming children after relatives and recording family names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people stopped weeping and sent portions to those with nothing prepared. Your line was joy is your strength. Today, the book that closes the Tanakh.

Three names, and no introduction. In the King James words, the book begins: "Adam, Sheth, Enosh." No "in the beginning", no setting, no verb. Just names, generation after generation, chapter after chapter. This is Chronicles, in Hebrew Divrei Hayamim, the words, or the events, of the days. In the order of books the Talmud lists, it comes last of all, so the Hebrew Bible, which opened with Adam in Genesis, comes back around to Adam at its end. A page of names can look like the part to skip. Today, let's not skip it.
screen: `ADAM, SHETH, ENOSH.` → `DIVREI HAYAMIM: THE EVENTS OF THE DAYS.` → `THE LAST BOOK STARTS AT THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Chronicles retells the whole story, and it starts by compressing Genesis into lists. Adam to Noah. Noah's sons. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom the book calls Israel. Then the tribes, one by one, with their families and towns. Why begin like this? A list of names says quickly what a story can't: nobody here came from nowhere. Every person stands at the end of a long line. And the lists aren't as dry as they look. Tucked into Judah's family is a man called Jabez. His mother named him that, the text says, because she bore him in pain. Then, in the middle of the list, Jabez calls out to God, asking to be blessed and kept from harm, and the text says God granted what he asked. One small prayer, buried in a genealogy, as if to say every name on this page had a life and a voice. Now look where the lists end up: at the people who came back from exile and settled again in Jerusalem, people like the ones we've met in Ezra and Nehemiah. So the chain runs from Adam to the returned exiles. One way to read it: the people rebuilding a small city after exile are placed inside a story as wide as humanity. A life can be lived as if it started with itself. Chronicles opens with a list that says otherwise.

882.title: Let him go up (2 Chronicles 36:23)
882.hook: the Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's call to go up and rebuild
882.howItsDone: In synagogue, being called up to say the blessings over the Torah reading is called an aliyah, a going up, and moving to the land of Israel is also called making aliyah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chronicles opened with three names: Adam, Sheth, Enosh. Your line was from Adam to now. Today, the last page of that same book, and the last words of the Hebrew Bible.

The second-to-last scene is a ruin. At the end of Second Chronicles, the Babylonians burn the house of God, break down the wall of Jerusalem, and carry the survivors away to Babylon. The land lay desolate and kept its sabbaths, the text says, as the word of the LORD by Jeremiah had said. If the book stopped there, the whole Hebrew Bible would close on smoke and exile. A new king, Cyrus of Persia, sends a proclamation through all his kingdom, in speech and in writing. And in the order this path follows, the last word of the whole Tanakh is a verb of movement.
screen: `THE HOUSE OF GOD BURNED.` → `THE PEOPLE CARRIED TO BABYLON.` → `THEN CYRUS SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the final verse, in the King James words: "Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, All the kingdoms of the earth hath the LORD God of heaven given me; and he hath charged me to build him an house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? The LORD his God be with him, and let him go up." And there it stops. In Hebrew, the very last word is ve-ya'al: and let him go up. Eight days ago we heard this same decree open the book of Ezra, and there the sentence keeps going: let him go up to Jerusalem, and build the house of the LORD. Chronicles stops one breath sooner. No Jerusalem yet, no building, no arrival. Just a question, a blessing, and the first step of a road. Some readers hear in it the word aliyah, a going up: being called up to the Torah in synagogue is an aliyah, and so is moving to the land of Israel. Now look back at this week. Ezra set his heart. Nehemiah's slow work was done before. The builders kept one hand on the stone. The Levites gave the sense. Joy became strength. Chronicles reached from Adam to now. And the whole library closes on let him go up: not with the building done, but with the call to keep climbing.
screen: `WHO IS THERE AMONG YOU?` · then, large: `LET HIM GO UP.` · `EZRA GOES ON; CHRONICLES STOPS.` · then: `A WEEK OF REBUILDING.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and hear Cyrus's question as if it were asked of you: who is there among you? Think of one place you've been stuck in the ruins a while, something left broken or put off, and choose one step up, small enough to take. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition for help to go up.
Ve-ya'al. And let him go up: the last words of the Hebrew Bible, Cyrus's call to the people, and let them go up and rebuild. Today's word.
Your line: the call to keep climbing. The road starts before the destination is on the page. That's day eight hundred eighty-two.
